newsitem.title: HONG KONG: S&P raises Hong Kong's credit ratings.
newsitem.headline: S&P raises Hong Kong's credit ratings.

text.p: Standard & Poor's Corp said on Wednesday that it has raised the foreign and local currency credit ratings of Hong Kong.
S&P said it raised Hong Kong's foreign currency ratings to A-plus/A-1-plus from single-A/A-1.
It also raised Hong Kong's local currency ratings to AA-minus/A-1-plus from A-plus/A-1.
The outlook is now stable, S&P said.
S&P said Hong Kong's upgrade is based on the improvement in China's ratings.
S&P raised China's foreign currency debt rating to BBB-plus from BBB on Wednesday.
The key factors underpinning the three-notch rating differential with China remain firmly in place as the transfer of sovereignty nears, S&P said.
Hong Kong reverts to Chinese rule on July 1.
"China's incentives to respect Hong Kong's autonomy will continue to be strong, especially as economic reforms in the mainland deepen," S&P said in a statement.

S&P said the rollback in some civil liberties in conjunction with the transfer in power has been factored into the ratings for some years and does not indicate any change in China's stance towards the territory.
"Indeed, Hong Kong's stable, conservative financial policies are an important buffer against political uncertainties," S&P said.
Barring any material change in its relations with China, Hong Kong's foreign currency ratings are expected to continue to move in tandem with China's in the long term, the rating agency said.

S&P said Hong Kong's ratings reflect the strong incentives for China to permit Hong Kong the strong degree of autonomy provided in the Basic Law, the Hong Kong government's very strong net creditor position and a wealthy and dynamic economy.

The Hong Kong dollar credit rating balances a stronger capacity to service local currency debt, due to the government's taxation powers and control of the domestic financial system, with the constraints imposed by the territory's tightening links with China.
The ratings also are constrained by the risk that misgovernance by Beijing could erode over time the pillars of Hong Kong's creditworthiness, S&P said.

Also constraining the ratings is the risk that, owing to the territory's economic and political integration with China, a potential deterioration in China's credit standing could, in turn, impair Hong Kong's credit standing, S&P said.
